chapter_theme: Pure Saivism (சுத்த சைவம்): the Lord who makes all things includes the four kinds of Saivism, and the pure Saiva is one who has discerned the real and the unreal, learned and practised in order, and passed through Vedanta and Siddhanta to the end of nada and the Supreme.
structure_note: 1419 introduces the four kinds of Saivism treated in this chapter and the next three; 1420 to 1422 describe the pure Saiva and the Siddhantin.

1419.reading: To consider the greatness of the all-knowing one who makes town and world alike is to see that Meru, the three worlds and the earth are his, and so are the four kinds of Saivism.
1419.nuance: நால்வகைச் சைவம், the four kinds of Saivism, are taken as the subjects of this chapter and the next three (pure, impure, path and severe pure). Line 3 (மூவுலகாளி யிலங்கெழுந்) is obscure, and how Meru and the worlds bear on the four kinds is unclear.

1420.reading: Pure Saivas, having discerned the real, the unreal and what is both, keeping clear of the sentient and the insentient and untouched by pure and impure, hold the eternal Supreme dear.
1420.nuance: சத்து, அசத்து and சதசத்து are in Siddhanta usually the Lord (real), the bonds (unreal) and the soul (real-unreal), and சித்து, அசித்து the sentient and insentient; that is the tradition's mapping, which the verse does not spell out. The pure Saiva is defined by discernment and by not being touched, not by outward marks.

1421.reading: Those who learn what is to be learned, go step by step through the true yoga in which the kalas abide and the knowledge of the earlier stages, reach the stage of the word and, rid of fault, see the Supreme beyond: they are the Saiva Siddhantins.
1421.nuance: முறைமுறை (in due order) makes the way a sequence: learning, yoga, knowledge, then the Supreme. முற்பத ஞானம் and சொற்பதம் are technical and can't be fixed here; சொற்பதம் may be the stage of the word or mantra, or the stage words can reach.

1422.reading: Those who have seen pure Vedanta, the clear Siddhanta and the end of nada have unwavering sight; those full in the end of nada, past the ends of the elements and of knowing, are lovers of knowledge.
1422.nuance: The verse is built on -அந்தம் (end): Vedanta, Siddhanta, Nadanta, Bhutanta, Bodhanta, traditionally a series of limits each passed in turn. Here Vedanta and Siddhanta stand together, not opposed. மாதுப் புனஞ்செய்ய is obscure.

links.note: Both make learning the start of a way that ends in seeing the true: the Kural's learners who see the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள்) take the road of no return; Tirumular's learn what is to be learned, then pass through yoga and knowledge to see the Supreme.

Both say those who saw Nadanta are unwavering (நாதாந்தங் கண்டோர் நடுக்கற்ற). 1422 sets Vedanta and Siddhanta side by side; 1435 distinguishes what the seers of Vedanta, of Nadanta and of Siddhanta each hold.

source_issues: 1419: line 3 (மூவுல காளி யிலங்கெழுந்) is obscure and may be corrupt.
1422: line 3 (புதாந்த போதாந்த மாதுப் புனஞ்செய்ய) is obscure; புதாந்த is probably பூதாந்த.
